statement: In two US national household surveys, about 9 in 100 people who had ever used cannabis had met, or were estimated to meet at some time in their life, criteria for cannabis dependence under older, narrower diagnostic definitions. In the National Comorbidity Survey (fieldwork 1990 to 1992; a probability sample of 8,098 people aged 15 to 54; response 82.4%; a standardized interview, the CIDI, given by lay interviewers), 46.3% of the population had ever used cannabis and 4.2% had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for cannabis dependence, so 9.1% (SE 0.7; about 7.7% to 10.5%, editors' calculation) of the people who had ever used it, even once, had ever been dependent by the time of the interview, against 23.1% for heroin, 16.7% for cocaine and 15.4% for alcohol in the same survey and 31.9% for tobacco (tobacco dependence was assessed, for daily smoking only, in a subsample of 4,414 and divided by tobacco use taken from another 1991 national survey, so it has no standard error); among people who had used cannabis, 12.0% of men and 5.5% of women had been dependent (Anthony et al., 1994). The dependence questions were asked only of people who reported at least several occasions of use, people who had started recently had had little time to become dependent, and the authors expect incomplete reporting, and the survey's leaving out people who had died, to lower the figures, while casual use that people forget or do not mention would push them the other way. In the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (interviews in 2001 to 2002 and 2004 to 2005; 7,389 adults who had ever used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence by a structured interview, the AUDADIS-IV), a survival analysis of recalled ages of first use and of onset estimated that 8.9% of people who used cannabis would become dependent at some time in their life (no interval given), 5.9% within 10 years of first use and about 2% within the first year, and half of the people who became dependent had done so within about 5 years of first use; the corresponding lifetime figures were 67.5% for nicotine, 22.7% for alcohol and 20.9% for cocaine (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). The figure of about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used, or about 1 in 10, that narrative reviews repeat is cited to these surveys or matches them (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, cite a 2006 book chapter for it, with their comparison figures from the 1990-92 survey; Volkow et al., 2014, and Curran et al., 2016, cite the 2001-05 analysis; Connor et al., 2021, the 1990-92 survey); the reviews' figures are second-hand. Two of these reviews also give about 1 in 10 for other groups without data of their own: Connor et al. (2021), citing a UN report, for people who use cannabis worldwide and for people who use it regularly, and Hall (2015), in its abstract, for people who use it regularly. DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence are narrower than DSM-5 cannabis use disorder, which needs 2 of 11 criteria within 12 months and includes mild cases (Connor et al., 2021). Higher figures from more recent US national data use other definitions and denominators: Connor et al. (2021) cite about 30% of people who use cannabis as developing a use disorder, without giving the measure (Hasin et al., 2015, not read here), and a 2020 professional statement gives 3 in 10 people who had used cannabis in the past year as meeting criteria for a use disorder (Page et al., 2020, citing a 2016 analysis of the 2012 to 2013 survey; second-hand); the pooled figures of a 2020 meta-analysis of general-population studies are given in the claim on cannabis strength and dependence. Both surveys are from the US, leave out people living in institutions, rely on what people recalled and reported, and predate legal markets and today's stronger products; figures by how often people use and by the age at which they started are in the claim on frequency and age of starting. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In two large US surveys, about 9 in 100 people who had ever tried cannabis, even once, had been dependent on it or were expected to become dependent at some point in their life, using an older, narrower definition of dependence. In the 1990 to 1992 survey this was fewer than for tobacco (about 32 in 100), heroin (23), cocaine (17) or alcohol (15), and more men (12 in 100) than women (about 6 in 100) who had used cannabis had been dependent. The 2001 to 2005 survey estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime and about 6 in 100 within 10 years of first use; for half of the people who became dependent, it began within about 5 years. Today's diagnosis, cannabis use disorder, also counts milder cases, and newer US figures, such as 3 in 10 among people who used in the past year, count only people using recently. Both surveys are from the US, from 1990 to 2005, before today's stronger products.
population: People in US national household surveys who had ever used cannabis: ages 15 to 54 in 1990 to 1992 (National Comorbidity Survey; 46.3% of 8,098 had used) and adults interviewed in 2001 to 2002 and 2004 to 2005 (NESARC; 7,389 who had used)
exposure: Any lifetime use of cannabis, even once (in the 1990-92 survey the dependence questions were asked only after at least several occasions of use)
comparator: None for the main figure (a share of everyone who had used); other substances in the same surveys
outcome: Lifetime DSM-III-R cannabis dependence as a proportion at interview (1990-92); lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV cannabis dependence after first use, by years since first use (2001-05)
magnitude: NCS 1990-92 (weighted, n = 8,098; Table 2): cannabis lifetime use 46.3% (SE 1.1), lifetime dependence 4.2% (0.3), dependence among people who had used 9.1% (0.7; editors' 95% CI about 7.7% to 10.5%); heroin 23.1% (5.6), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), alcohol 15.4% (0.7); tobacco 31.9% (no SE: dependence assessed in a subsample of 4,414, use taken from the 1991 NHSDA); among people who had used cannabis, men 12.0% (1.1), women 5.5% (0.7) (Table 5). NESARC 2001-05 (7,389 who had used cannabis; actuarial survival estimates, no intervals): lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence 8.9% (nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%); 5.9% within 10 years of first use; about 2% within the first year; half of the cases of dependence about 5 years after first use (a median among people who became dependent). Second-hand: about 1 in 10 of people who use regularly (Connor et al., 2021, citing a UN report; Hall, 2015, abstract); about 30% developing a use disorder in more recent US data, measure not given (Connor et al., 2021, citing Hasin et al., 2015); 3 in 10 people who used in the past year meeting criteria for a use disorder (Page et al., 2020, citing a 2016 analysis).

evidence.locator: Method and Materials, 1st paragraph (p. 245, continuing on p. 246); Diagnostic Assessment of Alcohol and Other Drug Dependence, 4th paragraph, and Analysis Procedures, 1st paragraph (p. 248)
evidence.extracted: National Comorbidity Survey: stratified multistage area probability sample of the noninstitutionalized civilian population aged 15 to 54 in the 48 coterminous US states, fieldwork 14 September 1990 to 6 February 1992, response rate 82.4%, 8,098 participants. Lifetime DSM-III-R dependence by the CIDI, scored by computer; the dependence questions were asked when people reported at least several occasions of extramedical use, on the assumption that dependence is very rare after no more than several uses. The proportion of people who had used a drug and became dependent equals the lifetime prevalence of dependence divided by the lifetime prevalence of use on at least one occasion.

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded. The 1990-92 survey is at low risk as a description of what it measured (JBI on card sc_anthony_1994: probability sample, response 82.4% with a non-response survey and weights, one standardized interview for all drug classes, design-based standard errors); its exclusions (institutions, deaths) and self-report would lower the figure, as its authors say, but not plausibly by much. The 2001-05 analysis is at moderate risk (card sc_lopez_quintero_2011: recalled ages, sometimes decades later; deaths and people in institutions excluded; lifetime estimates projected without intervals), but its lifetime figure agrees with the first survey's.

inconsistency.note: The two surveys measure different quantities (a proportion at one interview among everyone who had ever used, against a projected lifetime probability) and agree closely (9.1% and 8.9%). The higher figures the reviews cite use other definitions and denominators and are reported as such, not pooled.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: US household populations, 1990 to 2005, DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence, all stated in the claim; the gap to DSM-5 use disorder, to other countries and to today's products is stated, not assumed away.

imprecision.note: Standard error 0.7 points for the 1990-92 figure; no interval for the 2001-05 figures, but 7,389 people who had used cannabis.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to two national surveys.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (proportions in survey populations): starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3). Not downgraded: two independent national probability surveys, a decade apart and with different instruments and DSM versions, give about 9 in 100, and the claim states their measures, years and populations. Strict reading: the 2001-05 timing figures (5.9% within 10 years, about 2% in the first year, half of the cases within about 5 years) rest on recalled ages and an actuarial curve without intervals and on their own would be rated down one level for risk of bias, to very low. The narrative reviews and the 2020 professional statement are used only to trace the figure they repeat, to show the other denominators behind higher figures, and for the DSM-5 definition; they add no data, and the 30% and 3 in 10 they cite for newer data are second-hand and on other denominators and do not enter the rating. Overlap: Hall & Degenhardt (2009), Hall (2015) and Connor et al. (2021) take their 9% from the 1990-92 survey or a chapter by its first author (Connor's other 1 in 10 figures come from a UN report), and Volkow et al. (2014) and Curran et al. (2016) from the 2001-05 analysis, so the reviews are not further replication. Status replicated: the two surveys are independent and agree.
